questions.q: Which group lists only deities to whom the Vedic hymns were addressed?
questions.a: Indra, Agni and Ushas

questions.q: For how many generations, according to the chapter, have the Vedic texts been committed to memory and passed on orally?
questions.a: Anything between 100 and 200 generations

questions.q: Together with the seers, the Vedic deities sustained ritam. What is ritam?
questions.a: Truth and order in human life and in the cosmos
o: Truth and order in human life and in the cosmos
A daily offering made to Agni, the deity of fire
The divine Self that resides in every being
A collective gathering or assembly of a jana

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Rig Veda is the most ancient of the four Vedas.
Reason (R): Together with the seers, the Vedic deities sustained ritam, or truth and order in human life and in the cosmos.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) In which language did the rishis and rishikas compose the Vedic hymns?
(b) A famous Vedic hymn says 'ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti'. What does this line mean?
questions.a: (a) In an early form of the Sanskrit language. (b) 'The Existent (that is, the supreme reality) is one, but sages give it many names.'
s: (a) An early form of Sanskrit
(b) The Existent is one, but sages give it many names

questions.q:
The Vedas consist of thousands of hymns.
(a) What is a hymn, as the chapter describes it?
(b) The chapter calls the Vedas the most ancient texts of India. How does it place them among the texts of the whole world?
questions.a: (a) A hymn is a prayer in the form of a poem or song. (b) The Vedas are among the most ancient texts in the world.
s: (a) A prayer in the form of a poem or song
(b) Among the most ancient texts in the world

questions.q: True or False? 'The Rig Veda was composed less than 2,000 years ago.' Give the verdict and a reason worked out from the dates the chapter gives.
questions.a: False. Experts have proposed dates for the Rig Veda ranging from the 5th to the 2nd millennium BCE. Even the latest of these, the 2nd millennium BCE, ended in 1000 BCE, which is more than 3,000 years before today, so the Rig Veda is far older than 2,000 years.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: proposed dates run from the 5th to the 2nd millennium BCE; even the 2nd millennium BCE is over 3,000 years ago

questions.q:
Read these lines: 'Come together, speak together; common be your mind, may your thoughts agree.'
(a) Which Veda's last mantras call for this, according to the chapter?
(b) What do these lines call for among people?
(c) Name one other value that was especially important in the Vedic worldview.
questions.a: (a) The Rig Veda. (b) Unity among people. (c) Truth, which was often another name for God.
s: (a) The Rig Veda
(b) Unity among people
(c) Truth, often another name for God

questions.q:
During Heritage Week, a school in Varanasi sets up three stalls on the Vedas. Stall 1 has a chart with four boxes, three of them filled: 'Rig Veda', 'Yajur Veda', 'Sama Veda'; the fourth box is blank. Stall 2 plays a recording of Vedic chanting with a card: 'Recognised in 2008 by an organisation of the United Nations.' Stall 3 asks visitors to name the people who composed the hymns. A visitor asks why the school shows no handwritten copy of the hymns from the time they were composed.
(a) Fill the blank box on Stall 1's chart.
(b) Name the organisation on Stall 2's card, and say what it recognised Vedic chanting as.
(c) Answer Stall 3: what were the male and the female composers of the hymns called?
(d) Answer the visitor's question from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Atharva Veda. (b) UNESCO; it recognised Vedic chanting as 'a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity'. (c) Rishis (male seers) and rishikas (female seers). (d) The hymns were recited orally, not written: they were committed to memory through rigorous training and passed on by word of mouth, so there is no written copy from that time.
s: (a) Atharva Veda
(b) UNESCO; a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity
(c) Rishis and rishikas
(d) The hymns were memorised and passed on orally, not written

questions.q:
Your friend's notes on the Vedas contain five mistakes. Correct each one in a single line, using the chapter.
(a) 'The Vedas contain only a few short prayers.'
(b) 'As the hymns were passed on, they changed a great deal.'
(c) 'Pupils picked up the hymns casually, just by hearing them once.'
(d) 'In the chapter, the word cosmos means only the stars in the sky.'
(e) 'UNESCO is a body of the United Nations that promotes trade between nations.'
questions.a: (a) The Vedas consist of thousands of hymns. (b) They were passed on with hardly any alterations. (c) The hymns were committed to memory through rigorous training. (d) Cosmos means the world or the universe as an ordered and harmonious system. (e) UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, promotes dialogue between people and nations through education, science and culture.
s: (a) Thousands of hymns
(b) Hardly any alterations
(c) Memorised through rigorous training
(d) The world or universe as an ordered and harmonious system
(e) Promotes dialogue through education, science and culture

questions.q: What were the clans, or larger groups of people, of early Vedic society called?
questions.a: Janas

questions.q: On a class wall map of early Vedic society, one box holds the names Bharatas, Purus and Yadus. Which caption for the box fits the chapter?
questions.a: Some of the janas the Rig Veda lists, each associated with a particular region of the northwest of the Subcontinent
o: Some of the janas the Rig Veda lists, each associated with a particular region of the northwest of the Subcontinent
Some of the janas the Rig Veda lists, all living together in one region of the south of the Subcontinent
Some of the rishis who composed the Vedic hymns in the northwest of the Subcontinent
The assemblies through which the people of a jana met and governed themselves

questions.q:
Match each word in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Jana  2. Healer  3. Turvashas  4. Rig Veda
Column B: P. A clan, that is, a larger group of people  Q. Someone who uses traditional practices to relieve or heal diseases  R. One of the janas named in the chapter  S. The Vedic text that alone lists over 30 janas

Consider these statements about early Vedic society.
I. Each jana was associated with a particular region of the northwest part of the Subcontinent.
II. The words sabha and samiti both refer to a king or ruler.
III. Weavers, carpenters and barbers are among the professions mentioned in the Vedic texts.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q:
The Vedas give a few clues about how the janas governed their society.
(a) What did the word raja mean?
(b) What did the words sabha and samiti refer to?
questions.a: (a) A king or ruler. (b) Both refer to a collective gathering or assembly.
s: (a) A king or ruler
(b) A collective gathering or assembly

questions.q: True or False? 'The Bharatas and the Kurus are among the janas listed in the Rig Veda.' Give the verdict and add one more fact the chapter gives about the janas of the Rig Veda.
questions.a: True. The Rig Veda alone lists over 30 janas (such as the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus and Turvashas), each associated with a particular region of the northwest of the Subcontinent.
s: Verdict: True
One more fact: over 30 janas are listed, or each was linked to a region of the northwest, or another named jana

questions.a: (a) Any two of weaver, potter, builder, carpenter. (b) Healer. (c) Dancer.
s: (a) Any two of weaver, potter, builder, carpenter
(b) Healer
(c) Dancer

questions.q: A pupil writes: 'In the early Vedic janas, one king alone took every decision, and the people had no say at all.' Test this claim against the chapter. Give three points.
questions.a: The claim goes beyond the chapter. (1) The chapter says not much is known of how the janas governed their society; the Vedas give only a few clues. (2) One clue is the word raja, a king or ruler, so there were rulers. (3) But the Vedas also use sabha and samiti, both meaning a collective gathering or assembly, which suggests people also met together; so the chapter cannot support 'one king alone' or 'no say at all'.
s: States that little is known; the Vedas give only a few clues
Raja shows there were rulers
Sabha and samiti point to collective assemblies, so the claim is not supported

questions.q:
Class 6 in Ambala is setting up a 'Work in a Vedic jana' corner at the school fair. There is room for exactly 6 stalls. Each stall must show a profession that the chapter says is mentioned in the Vedic texts, and the school nurse, who is helping, wants one stall on a profession linked with health. Pupils have proposed 9 stalls: agriculturist, weaver, potter, goldsmith, carpenter, healer, shopkeeper, barber and priest.
(a) Which two proposals cannot be confirmed from the chapter's list of professions?
(b) Does this prove that there were no goldsmiths or shopkeepers in Vedic times? Explain from the way the chapter words its list.
(c) After those two are removed, how many proposals are left, and how many more must be dropped?
(d) Which remaining stall must NOT be the one dropped, and why?
questions.a: (a) Goldsmith and shopkeeper. (b) No. The chapter lists the professions 'such as agriculturist, weaver, potter, builder, carpenter, healer, dancer, barber, priest, etc.', so the list gives examples and is not complete; the chapter cannot confirm these two, but it does not say they did not exist. (c) 9 - 2 = 7 are left, and 7 - 6 = 1 more must be dropped. (d) The healer stall must stay: it is the only proposal linked with health, since a healer uses traditional practices to relieve or heal diseases. Any one of the other six (agriculturist, weaver, potter, carpenter, barber, priest) may be dropped.
s: (a) Goldsmith and shopkeeper
(b) No: the list says 'such as ... etc.', so it gives examples only and cannot rule them out
(c) 7 left; 1 more must be dropped
(d) Keep the healer, the only health profession; any other one may go

questions.q: Imagine you are a historian whose only evidence about early Vedic society is what the Vedic texts say. Write four points, one on each of the following, saying what the texts tell you and, where it applies, what they leave unclear: (1) how society was organised; (2) where the groups lived; (3) how they were governed; (4) the work people did.
questions.a: (1) Society was organised in janas or clans; the Rig Veda alone lists over 30, such as the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus, Yadus and Turvashas. (2) Each jana was associated with a particular region of the northwest part of the Subcontinent. (3) Not much is known of how the janas governed their society; the texts give only a few clues, so the details of government stay unclear. (4) The texts mention many professions, such as agriculturist, weaver, potter, builder, carpenter, healer, dancer, barber and priest.
s: (1) Janas or clans; over 30 listed in the Rig Veda, with an example
(2) Each jana linked to a region of the northwest
(3) Not much is known; the texts give only a few clues, so how they governed is unclear
(4) Names several professions from the Vedic texts

questions.q: Which two new concepts did the Upanishads introduce, building upon Vedic ideas?
questions.a: Rebirth and karma

questions.q: What does the mantra 'aham brahmasmi' mean?
questions.a: I am brahman

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the Vedanta school, brahman is not to be confused with the god Brahma.
Reason (R): In the Vedanta school, brahman is the one divine essence that everything (human life, nature and the universe) is, and not one particular god.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the Vedic schools of thought.
I. Daily Vedic rituals were generally prayers and offerings to Agni, and these rituals became more and more complex over time.
II. Brahman is sometimes called simply tat, meaning 'that'.
III. Yoga was a school of thought that did not accept the authority of the Vedas.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
(a) Name the school of thought that teaches that everything (human life, nature and the universe) is one divine essence called brahman.
(b) What does the prayer beginning 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah' wish?
questions.a: (a) Vedanta. (b) 'May all creatures be happy'; it goes on to wish them all to be free from disease and sorrow.
s: (a) Vedanta
(b) That all creatures be happy and free from disease and sorrow

questions.q:
Yoga is a different school of thought from Vedanta, yet the chapter counts both among the Vedic schools of thought.
(a) Give the fact about Yoga's beginnings that places it among the Vedic schools.
(b) Show how Yoga's aim depends on an idea that the Vedanta school teaches.
questions.a: (a) Early in the 1st millennium BCE, Yoga was one of several schools of thought that grew out of the Vedas (together they became the foundations of what we call Hinduism today). (b) Yoga developed methods to achieve the realisation of brahman in one's consciousness, and brahman is the Vedanta idea of the one divine essence that everything is; so Yoga's aim is built on that Vedantic idea.
s: (a) It grew out of the Vedas early in the 1st millennium BCE
(b) Its aim, realising brahman in one's consciousness, uses Vedanta's idea of brahman as the one divine essence

questions.q:
Answer from the story 'Shvetaketu and the seed of reality'.
(a) Why was Shvetaketu sent to a gurukula?
(b) Why did his father Uddalaka decide to test him, and on what subject were the questions?
(c) Give one example Uddalaka used to explain that brahman, though invisible, is everywhere.
questions.a: (a) To learn the Vedas. (b) Uddalaka realised that his son had become very proud of his learning; he tested him with questions on the nature of brahman, which Shvetaketu could not answer. (c) The seed of a banyan fruit seems empty but already contains the future banyan tree; or all kinds of different pots can be made out of the same clay.
s: (a) To learn the Vedas
(b) He had become very proud of his learning; questions on the nature of brahman
(c) The banyan seed or the pots made of the same clay

questions.q: Compare how Nachiketa and Gargi got their answers. For each, say (a) what the questioner wanted to know, (b) what the questioner did after the one being asked held back, and (c) what was finally explained.
questions.a: (a) Nachiketa wanted to know what happens after the death of the body; Gargi asked a series of questions on the nature of the world and finally on the nature of brahman. (b) When Yama tried to avoid answering, Nachiketa persisted; when Yajnavalkya asked Gargi to stop, she later resumed her questions. (c) Yama explained that the atman is hidden within all creatures and is immortal, neither born nor dying; Yajnavalkya explained how brahman makes the world, the seasons, the rivers and everything else possible.
s: (a) Nachiketa: what happens after death of the body; Gargi: the nature of the world and of brahman
(b) Nachiketa persisted; Gargi resumed her questions
(c) Atman is immortal; brahman makes the world, seasons and rivers possible

questions.q:
A storytelling club in Mysuru has one 25-minute slot at the school festival. It has rehearsed three Upanishadic stories: the Shvetaketu story takes 12 minutes, the Nachiketa story takes 10 minutes and the Gargi-Yajnavalkya story takes 15 minutes. The festival theme is 'Asking questions matters, whether you are a man, a woman or a child', and the club wants its stories to show at least one woman and at least one child as the questioner.
(a) From which Upanishad does the Nachiketa story come?
(b) What did Nachiketa learn from Yama?
(c) Who announced a prize in the Gargi story, and for what?
(d) Which two stories should the club tell? Justify using the timings and the theme.
questions.a: (a) The Katha Upanishad. (b) That the atman, or self, is hidden within all creatures, is neither born nor dies, and is immortal. (c) The wise king Janaka, for the winner of a philosophical debate. (d) Nachiketa and Gargi: 10 + 15 = 25 minutes, which exactly fills the slot, and it shows a boy (Nachiketa) and a rishika (Gargi) asking the questions. Shvetaketu and Gargi would take 12 + 15 = 27 minutes, which is too long. Shvetaketu and Nachiketa would take 12 + 10 = 22 minutes, which fits the time, but has no woman questioner, and in the Shvetaketu story it is the father who asks the questions.
s: (a) Katha Upanishad
(b) The atman is immortal, neither born nor dying
(c) King Janaka, for the winner of a philosophical debate
(d) Nachiketa and Gargi: 25 minutes with a boy and a woman questioning; 27 is too long and 22 has no woman

questions.q: A pupil asks: 'If the Vedanta school is right, why should anyone pray for the happiness of all creatures, and not only for their own family?' Answer her in five linked steps, using the chapter's ideas of brahman, the two mantras, atman and the prayer 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah'.
questions.a: (1) Vedanta teaches that everything (human life, nature and the universe) is one divine essence, brahman. (2) 'Aham brahmasmi', 'I am brahman', says I am divine. (3) 'Tat tvam asi', 'You are That', says the other person is that same essence too. (4) The Upanishads add that the atman, the Self in every being, is ultimately one with brahman, so it follows that everything is connected and interdependent. (5) So the happiness of every creature is linked with one's own, which is why the common prayer 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah' asks that all creatures be happy and free from disease and sorrow, not just one's family.
s: (1) Everything is one divine essence, brahman
(2) Aham brahmasmi: I am brahman, I am divine
(3) Tat tvam asi: You are That, others share the same essence
(4) Atman in every being is one with brahman, so everything is connected and interdependent
(5) Concludes that this is why the prayer wishes happiness for all creatures

questions.q: On his chariot ride through the city at the age of 29, which person did Siddhartha see who appeared happy and at peace?
questions.a: An ascetic

questions.q: Under which tree at Bodh Gaya did Siddhartha meditate for many days before he attained enlightenment?
questions.a: A pipal tree

questions.q: At Bodh Gaya, Siddhartha realised what the source of human suffering is. What did he realise?
questions.a: Avidya (ignorance) and attachment are the source of human suffering
o: Avidya (ignorance) and attachment are the source of human suffering
Old age and sickness alone are the source of human suffering
Living in a palace is the source of human suffering
Not performing yajnas is the source of human suffering

questions.q:
Match each word in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Lumbini  2. Bodh Gaya  3. Avidya  4. Bhikshuni
Column B: P. Ignorance  Q. A nun of the Sangha  R. The place where Siddhartha Gautama was born  S. The place where he attained enlightenment

(a) What was the Sangha founded by the Buddha?
(b) Who were its members at first, and who joined later?
questions.a: (a) A community of people who dedicated themselves to practising and spreading the Buddha's teachings. (b) At first bhikshus, or monks; later bhikshunis, or nuns.
s: (a) A community dedicated to practising and spreading his teachings
(b) Monks (bhikshus) first, nuns (bhikshunis) later

questions.q: True or False? 'Siddhartha Gautama, who became the Buddha, was born about two and a half thousand years ago, in a place that is today in Nepal.' Give the verdict and the detail from the chapter that supports it.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that about two-and-a-half millenniums ago, the young prince Siddhartha Gautama was born in Lumbini, which is today in Nepal.
s: Verdict: True
Support: born about two-and-a-half millenniums ago in Lumbini, today in Nepal

questions.q:
The Buddha taught ahimsa, which is generally translated as 'non-violence'.
(a) What does ahimsa originally mean?
(b) Ravi says, 'Ahimsa only means not fighting wars.' Use the original meaning to show why Ravi's idea is too narrow.
questions.a: (a) 'Non-hurting' or 'non-injuring'. (b) Non-hurting covers hurting or injuring anyone at any time, not only in war; for example, injuring an animal or hurting a classmate would also go against ahimsa.
s: (a) Non-hurting or non-injuring
(b) Explains that it covers any hurting or injuring, not only war, with an example

questions.q: A pupil writes: 'Siddhartha left the palace because he was unhappy with his family.' Test this claim against the chapter's account. Give three points.
questions.a: The claim is not supported. (1) At 29, on a chariot ride, he saw for the first time an old man, a sick man and a dead body. (2) He also saw an ascetic who appeared happy and at peace. (3) Following this experience he gave up palace life and searched for the root cause of suffering in human life; the chapter says nothing about him being unhappy with his family.
s: Saw an old man, a sick man and a dead body for the first time at 29
Saw an ascetic who seemed happy and at peace
Left to search for the root cause of suffering, not because of his family; claim rejected

questions.q:
A school in Gaya holds a 'Kindness Fortnight'. Its notice board shows two sayings of the Buddha: 'Not by water is one made pure, though many people may bathe here. But one is pure in whom truth and dharma reside.' and 'Conquering oneself is greater than conquering a thousand men on the battlefield a thousand times.' In week 1, Class 6 records 14 complaints of pushing and name-calling. After daily talks on not hurting others, week 2 has 5 complaints.
(a) According to the first saying, what does NOT make a person pure?
(b) According to the first saying, in whom does purity reside?
(c) What kind of discipline does the second saying stress?
(d) By how many did the complaints fall from week 1 to week 2, and which teaching of the Buddha were the daily talks about?
questions.a: (a) Bathing in water (in sacred rivers), even though many people bathe there. (b) In a person in whom truth and dharma reside. (c) A sincere inner discipline: conquering oneself. (d) 14 - 5 = 9 fewer complaints; the talks were about ahimsa, not hurting others.
s: (a) Bathing in water, as many people do, does not make one pure
(b) In one in whom truth and dharma reside
(c) Sincere inner discipline, conquering oneself
(d) Fell by 9; the teaching is ahimsa

questions.q:
The chapter says the Buddha's influence on India and Asia 'is still perceptible today'. Kunal disagrees: 'His influence faded within a few hundred years of his life.' Test Kunal's claim with the chapter's dates. Take the 6th century CE as about 1,500 years ago and the 10th century CE as about 1,100 years ago.
(a) About how many years ago was Siddhartha Gautama born, according to the chapter?
(b) A stone panel showing the Buddha teaching is some 1,800 years old. About how many years after his birth was it made?
(c) The rock-cut caves at Ellora, some of them Buddhist, were cut between the 6th and the 10th centuries CE. About how many years after his birth was that?
(d) Is Kunal right? Decide, using your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) About 2,500 years ago (two-and-a-half millenniums). (b) 2,500 - 1,800 = about 700 years after his birth. (c) 2,500 - 1,500 = 1,000 and 2,500 - 1,100 = 1,400, so about 1,000 to 1,400 years after his birth. (d) No. About 700 years after his birth, artists were still carving him teaching, and 1,000 to 1,400 years after it, Buddhist caves were still being cut at Ellora. His influence lasted far longer than a few hundred years, which fits the chapter's statement that it is still perceptible today.
s: (a) About 2,500 years ago
(b) About 700 years after his birth
(c) About 1,000 to 1,400 years after his birth
(d) Kunal is wrong: the panel and the Ellora caves show the influence lasting 700 to 1,400 years and more

questions.q: At what age did Prince Vardhamana leave his home to go in search of spiritual knowledge?
In Jain teaching, what does aparigraha mean?
questions.a: Non-possession: detachment from material possessions, limiting oneself to what is truly necessary
o: Non-possession: detachment from material possessions, limiting oneself to what is truly necessary
Non-hurting: not injuring any living creature in deed or in thought
Many aspects: the truth cannot be fully described by any single statement
Conquest: winning over ignorance and attachments to reach enlightenment

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Charvaka school believed that there can be no life after death.
Reason (R): The Charvaka school gained great popularity and spread across the land.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. The word 'Jain' comes from jina, which means 'great hero'.
II. Jainism became widespread at the same time as Buddhism, although its roots are said to be much more ancient.
III. The caves cut into the rock at Ellora between the 6th and the 10th centuries CE include Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q:
(a) What does the Jain idea of anekantavada mean?
(b) Give one everyday example that shows this idea.
questions.a: (a) 'Not just one' aspect or perspective: the truth has many aspects and cannot be fully described by any single statement. (b) Any fitting example, such as two pupils describing the same building, one from the front and one from the back, each giving a true but partial description.
s: (a) Truth has many aspects and no single statement describes it fully
(b) A fitting everyday example of partial but true views

questions.q:
Meher says: 'Spreading teachings far and wide was a Buddhist practice only; Jain monks never left their own towns.'
(a) Correct Meher, using the chapter.
(b) Name the two kinds of place where such travelling monks lived, and one trace of them that archaeologists have found.
questions.a: (a) In both Buddhism and Jainism, monks, and sometimes nuns too, travelled across the land to spread their teachings far and wide. (b) Some created new monasteries in faraway places, while others led ascetic lives in caves cut in the rock; archaeologists have found traces of those monasteries, and sometimes even the names of the monks who lived in the rock-cut caves and the stone beds they slept on.
s: (a) Monks (and sometimes nuns) of both Buddhism and Jainism travelled to spread their teachings
(b) Monasteries in faraway places and rock-cut caves; a trace such as monks' names or stone beds

questions.q:
Answer from the Jain story of Rohineya.
(a) Who was Rohineya?
(b) When he was arrested, what did he pretend to be?
(c) What did he do after he felt remorseful?
questions.a: (a) An extraordinarily skilled burglar who evaded all attempts to catch him. (b) A simple farmer. (c) He went to Mahavira, confessed his crimes, returned the stolen treasures and asked for forgiveness; he became a monk.
s: (a) A very skilled burglar
(b) A simple farmer
(c) Confessed to Mahavira, returned the treasures, asked forgiveness and became a monk

questions.q: The chapter compares Indian culture to an ancient tree with many roots, a common trunk and many branches. Explain what each part stands for, with one example from the chapter: (a) the roots, (b) the trunk, (c) the branches.
questions.a: (a) The roots are the many cultural roots, such as the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools of thought (and folk and tribal traditions). (b) The trunk is what these schools share despite their differences: concepts such as dharma, karma, rebirth, the search for an end to suffering and ignorance, and many important values. (c) The branches are the different manifestations of Indian culture, such as art, literature, science, medicine, religion, the art of governance and martial arts.
s: (a) Roots: the many schools of thought and traditions, with an example
(b) Trunk: shared concepts such as dharma, karma and rebirth
(c) Branches: manifestations such as art, literature, science or medicine

questions.q:
Class 6C in Jaipur, with 32 pupils, starts a 'Need, not want' month. Together the pupils own 410 pens and pencils. A survey shows that each pupil uses about 3 pens and pencils a month. Two plans are proposed: in Plan X each pupil keeps 3 and the rest are donated to a village school; in Plan Y each pupil keeps 5 and the rest are donated.
(a) Which Jain teaching is the 'Need, not want' month based on, and what does it mean?
(b) How many pens and pencils would be donated under Plan X?
(c) Under Plan Y, how many would the class keep, and how many more is that than the class needs in a month?
(d) Which plan fits that Jain teaching better? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) Aparigraha, 'non-possession': detachment from material possessions, limiting oneself to what is truly necessary. (b) 32 x 3 = 96 kept, so 410 - 96 = 314 donated. (c) 32 x 5 = 160 kept, which is 160 - 96 = 64 more than the 96 needed in a month. (d) Plan X: each pupil keeps exactly the 3 a month they need (96 in all) and 314 are donated, whereas Plan Y keeps 64 more than needed and donates only 410 - 160 = 250. Plan X limits possessions to what is truly necessary.
s: (a) Aparigraha, non-possession: keep only what is truly necessary
(b) 314 donated
(c) 160 kept, 64 more than needed
(d) Plan X: keeps only the 96 needed and donates 314 against 250

questions.q: Compare Buddhism and Jainism as the chapter presents them, and analyse what they share and where they differ. Use five points: (1) the founders' family background and birthplaces; (2) the age at which each left home and why; (3) how each reached supreme wisdom and the title each received; (4) their main teachings; (5) their relationship with the Vedic schools.
questions.a: (1) Both founders were born into royal families: Siddhartha Gautama in Lumbini (today in Nepal), Vardhamana near Vaishali in modern Bihar. (2) Siddhartha left at 29, after seeing an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a peaceful ascetic; Vardhamana left at 30 in search of spiritual knowledge. (3) Siddhartha attained enlightenment after meditating under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya and became the 'Buddha' (enlightened or awakened one); Vardhamana achieved 'infinite knowledge' after 12 years of ascetic discipline and became 'Mahavira' (great hero). (4) Both taught ahimsa; the Jain ideas anekantavada and aparigraha are, the chapter says, shared to a large extent with Buddhism (and the Vedantic school); the Buddha's own stress was on ignorance and attachment as the source of suffering, and on a sincere inner discipline. (5) Both departed from the authority of the Vedas, yet they shared with the Vedic schools concepts such as dharma, karma, rebirth and the search for an end to suffering and ignorance.
s: (1) Both royal; Lumbini and near Vaishali
(2) Left at 29 after the four sights; at 30 for spiritual knowledge
(3) Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, 'Buddha'; 12 years of discipline, 'Mahavira'
(4) Both taught ahimsa; anekantavada and aparigraha largely shared with Buddhism; the Buddha stressed ignorance, attachment and inner discipline
(5) Both departed from Vedic authority but shared dharma, karma, rebirth and ending suffering

questions.q: According to official figures, about how many tribes did India have in 2011?
Which deity, worshipped at Puri in Odisha, was originally a tribal deity according to tradition?
questions.a: Jagannath

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Donyipolo  2. Khandoba  3. Singbonga  4. Todas
Column B: P. A supreme deity, worshipped by the Munda and Santhal tribals among others, who created this whole world  Q. A combined form of the Sun and the Moon, worshipped by several tribes of Arunachal Pradesh  R. Tribal people of the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu, for whom over thirty peaks are homes of gods and goddesses  S. A god of parts of central India who rose to the status of a supreme god

Assertion (A): Most anthropologists today still describe tribes as 'primitive' or 'inferior', as many did in the 19th century.
Reason (R): Deeper studies of tribal communities have brought out their rich and complex cultures.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
Classify each tradition below as a folk tradition or a tribal tradition, and give the chapter's reason. Say also what makes each an oral tradition.
(a) In a fishing village on the coast, ordinary fishing families teach their children boat songs by singing them together while rowing.
(b) In a tribe living in the forests of Jharkhand, the elders teach the children their festival dances by dancing with them.
questions.a: (a) A folk tradition, because it is transmitted by common people. (b) A tribal tradition, because it is transmitted by a tribe. Both are oral traditions, since they are passed on through everyday practice, without written texts.
s: (a) Folk: passed on by common people, through practice without written texts
(b) Tribal: passed on by a tribe, through practice without written texts

questions.q: True or False? 'Even though tribes generally worship many deities linked with nature, many tribal groups also have a concept of a higher divinity or supreme being.' Give the verdict and support it with one example from the chapter.
questions.a: True. For example, several tribes of Arunachal Pradesh worship Donyipolo, a combined form of the Sun and the Moon who rose to the status of a supreme god; the Munda and Santhal worship Singbonga, a supreme deity who created the world; Khandoba in parts of central India also rose to that status.
s: Verdict: True
Example: Donyipolo, Singbonga or Khandoba as a supreme deity

questions.q:
Folk, tribal and Hindu belief systems share some concepts about nature.
(a) Name any three elements of nature that all three regard as sacred.
(b) What reason does the chapter give for regarding them as sacred?
(c) How does this idea explain why tribes generally worship many deities?
questions.a: (a) Any three of mountains, rivers, trees, plants, animals and some stones. (b) There is consciousness behind all of them. (c) Since each natural element has consciousness behind it, tribes worship many deities, each associated with such natural elements.
s: (a) Any three of mountains, rivers, trees, plants, animals, stones
(b) There is consciousness behind all of them
(c) Many deities, each linked with a natural element

questions.q:
A museum in Bhubaneswar is planning a 'Tribal Roots' gallery with four panels. Panel 1 will explain what a tribe is. Panel 2 shows the line: 'In its Hindi text, the Constitution of India calls tribes ______.' Panel 3 shows two figures for 2011: 705 tribes and about 104 million tribal people. Panel 4, titled 'From many gods to one supreme god', has room for only one deity, and the curator must choose between Jagannath and Singbonga.
(a) Write the definition of a tribe that anthropologists usually give today, for Panel 1.
(b) Fill the blank on Panel 2, and give the two English terms the Constitution uses.
(c) To help visitors picture 104 million people, with which countries' populations does the chapter compare it?
(d) Which deity should go on Panel 4? Justify your choice from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A group of families or clans sharing a tradition of common descent, a culture and a language, living as a close-knit community under a chief and holding no private property. (b) Janjati; in English it uses 'tribes' and 'tribal communities'. (c) It is more than the populations of Australia and the United Kingdom together. (d) Singbonga: the Munda and Santhal worship him as a supreme deity who created this whole world, which fits the title. Jagannath is the chapter's example of a tribal deity taken into wider worship at Puri, which shows exchange between traditions rather than the rise to one supreme god.
s: (a) Families or clans with common descent, culture and language, close-knit, under a chief, no private property
(b) Janjati; 'tribes' and 'tribal communities' in English
(c) More than Australia and the United Kingdom together
(d) Singbonga, a supreme deity who created the world; Jagannath shows exchange instead

questions.q: Arav argues: 'Ancient India had no word for "tribe". So there were no tribal communities in ancient India; they appeared only in modern times.' Evaluate his argument in four steps: (1) what the chapter says about the word; (2) what tribes were in ancient India; (3) how the chapter's account of early Vedic society and today's definition of a tribe fit together; (4) your verdict on his conclusion.
questions.a: (1) He is right about the word: ancient India did not have a word for 'tribe'. (2) But tribes did exist: they were just different janas that lived in a specific environment, such as forests or mountains. (3) Early Vedic society itself was organised in janas, or clans, that is, larger groups of people, and today anthropologists define a tribe as a group of families or clans sharing common descent, a culture and a language. So a forest or mountain jana of ancient times is what we now call a tribe. (4) His conclusion does not follow: having no separate word does not mean the people did not exist; they were simply counted as janas, like other groups.
s: (1) Agrees that ancient India had no word for 'tribe'
(2) Tribes were janas living in a specific environment such as forests or mountains
(3) Links janas (clans) with today's definition (families or clans with common descent, culture, language)
(4) Verdict: the conclusion fails; no word does not mean no tribes

questions.q:
For a project on Andre Beteille's statement about tribal religions and Hinduism, Riya collected four examples from the chapter:
E1: According to tradition, Jagannath, worshipped at Puri, was originally a tribal deity.
E2: Various forms of the mother-goddess worshipped across India were also originally tribal.
E3: Some tribes adopted Hindu deities long ago.
E4: Some tribes possess their own versions of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana.
She concludes: 'Three of my four examples show tribes taking from Hinduism, so the influence ran mostly one way, and Beteille was wrong to call the other direction "equally true".'
Evaluate her conclusion in five steps: (1) sort out the examples of Hinduism being influenced by tribal religions; (2) sort out the examples of tribes being influenced by Hinduism; (3) check her count; (4) say whether a handful of examples can settle the question, using what the chapter says about the exchange; (5) give your verdict and the result the chapter draws.
questions.a: (1) E1 and E2 show Hinduism influenced by tribal religions: 2 examples. (2) E3 and E4 show tribes influenced by Hinduism: 2 examples. (3) Her count is wrong: it is 2 and 2, not 3 out of 4. (4) A few examples cannot settle it, since the chapter gives them only 'for instance'; it says deities, concepts, legends and rituals have been freely exchanged in both directions, and Beteille says castes and tribes have influenced each other since the beginning of history and before. (5) Her conclusion fails and Beteille's statement stands: the influence ran both ways, and the chapter says the result of this long interaction has been mutual enrichment, so folk and tribal beliefs count among India's cultural roots.
s: (1) E1 and E2: Hinduism influenced by tribal religions
(2) E3 and E4: tribes influenced by Hinduism
(3) The count is 2 and 2, so her 'three of four' is wrong
(4) Examples are only instances; the chapter says exchange ran freely in both directions
(5) Verdict: conclusion fails; result is mutual enrichment, tribal beliefs are among India's cultural roots
